Queue workers on Citadel#

Laravel apps on Citadel dispatch jobs to a queue, but the platform runs no queue worker: one container per app, Apache in front, and nothing that keeps a long-lived php artisan queue:work alive. A queue with no worker is a promise with no keeper. This page covers what works today (a short worker driven by the scheduler), how a release restarts workers, what has not been tested yet, and the request text for the supervised worker we want from the Citadel team. Finish Citadel setup first if the app is not wired up yet.

What works today#

Laravel's own guidance is that a permanent queue:work needs a process monitor to keep it running (queues), and Citadel has none. So the worker rides the one thing every app already runs: the scheduler's single cron entry, which runs as the app user each minute (scheduling). An app that already schedules tasks has this entry; the worker reuses it, so nothing new runs on the server.

* * * * * cd /path-to-your-project && php artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1

The schedule then starts a short worker every minute. In routes/console.php (Laravel 11+, where the scheduling docs put the task schedule):

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schedule;

Schedule::command('queue:work --stop-when-empty --max-time=50')
    ->everyMinute()
    ->withoutOverlapping(10);

Each piece is documented:

  • --stop-when-empty processes all jobs and then exits gracefully, the option Laravel documents for a container that should shut down once the queue is empty (queues).
  • --max-time=50 caps a run at 50 seconds, so a run started before a release cannot outlive the code it booted with (queues).
  • everyMinute() runs the task on each scheduler tick (scheduling).
  • withoutOverlapping(10) skips the tick while the previous run is still going. The lock lives in the cache and expires after 24 hours by default; the explicit 10-minute expiry bounds a lock that a crashed run leaves behind (scheduling).

Because every run boots fresh and exits, there is no stale code and no memory growth between runs. The trade is latency: a job waits for the next minute tick, and a busy queue drains one burst per minute.

Apps that Sourdough generates in its Laravel shapes ship this already, behind one switch. config/worker.php reads QUEUE_WORKER_MODE: scheduler (the .env.example default) schedules the short worker above, and none schedules nothing, for an app whose worker a supervisor or a separate container runs. Their task adds --tries=3, so a failing job stops after three attempts instead of retrying on every tick (queues), and tests/Feature/QueueWorkerScheduleTest.php checks both modes. An app built by hand can copy the same three pieces.

Warning

Keep every job's timeout below its connection's retry_after, at least several seconds shorter. If a job is still processing past retry_after, the connection releases it back onto the queue and another run picks it up, so the job runs twice. The worker's --timeout is 60 seconds by default, the shipped retry_after is 90, and a job may name its own timeout with the Timeout attribute (worker timeouts, job expiration). Job timeouts need the PCNTL extension in the image (max job attempts and timeout). Give jobs a finite number of tries: --tries=0 retries forever, and a permanently failing job would then spin the queue every minute.

With the database driver the jobs live in a table that Laravel's default migration creates (0001_01_01_000002_create_jobs_table); an app without it generates one with php artisan make:queue-table (queues).

Deploys#

Workers do not notice new code until they restart, so a release restarts them (queue workers and deployment). Laravel documents two commands, and the current release has both:

  • php artisan queue:restart tells every worker to exit gracefully after its current job, so no job in flight is lost. The restart signal is stored in the cache, so the app needs a working cache driver.
  • php artisan reload terminates the long-running services (queue workers, Reverb, Octane) in one command; outside Laravel Cloud you configure the process monitor that restarts them yourself (deployment).

For the short worker above, the restart is mostly belt-and-braces: a run started before the release ends within its 50-second cap regardless, and the command makes sure it ends now instead of finishing the rest of the window on old code. For a supervised worker the restart is the whole mechanism, because the process never exits on its own.

Squire's scripts/release.sh does this for you in its Laravel block, after laravel migrate and laravel optimize and before the Oracle check and the smoke test: the code is checked out and optimized, the smoke test has not run yet, and a worker restarted here comes up on the new code before the release declares success. The step runs php artisan reload where Laravel has it, and otherwise queue:restart and schedule:interrupt, each only when that command exists. It is report only (a failed restart is a warning), and SQUIRE_ARTISAN_RESTART=0 turns it off. See The release script for the step order.

Off Citadel: a worker process type#

On a platform that runs more than one process per app (OpenShift, Coolify, raw Docker), the worker is its own container from the same image: The portable image runs as worker (php artisan queue:work --tries=3 --max-time=3600 --sleep=3, the command the request below asks Citadel for) and as scheduler (php artisan schedule:work), picked by SQUIRE_ROLE. The scheduler there sets QUEUE_WORKER_MODE=none, so the short worker above is not scheduled beside the real one. A deploy replaces the containers, so no restart signal is needed, and the timeout rule above holds on both paths.

Not yet tested on Citadel#

The short worker is the stack's plan, not a measured fact: the combination of --stop-when-empty, --max-time and withoutOverlapping puts three documented features together, and it has not been run on Citadel yet. How fast a queue actually drains, how the cron entry behaves on the platform, and what the logs look like are all unmeasured, and the Citadel test is tracked separately; this page will say what it found when it lands.

The supervised worker we are asking for#

The text below is ready to send to the Citadel team. It asks for the long-lived worker Laravel expects, with the restart hook that makes deploys safe.

Request: a supervised queue worker per app

We would like a supported way to run one long-lived process per app, kept alive by a process monitor that restarts it when it exits.

What it runs:

    php artisan queue:work --sleep=3 --tries=3 --max-time=3600

One worker per app, more where an app needs the throughput.

Why: Laravel's queue worker is a long-lived process that a process monitor must keep running, and it does not pick up new code until it is restarted. Today our apps run a short worker from the scheduler every minute, which works but is a stopgap: a job waits up to a minute for the next tick, a run that fills its minute overlaps the next one (the overlap guard then skips ticks and adds more delay), and the framework reboots every tick.

Restart on deploy: the Quick Update post-script (where scripts/release.sh already runs) would call php artisan reload, which terminates the worker after its current job finishes; the monitor then starts it again on the new code. The stop is graceful: on SIGTERM the worker finishes the job it is processing before it exits.

Timeouts: each job's timeout stays below the connection's retry_after (at least several seconds shorter), so a frozen job is killed before the queue retries it and runs twice. The image needs the PCNTL extension for job timeouts.

Logs: worker output where the app's other logs are, viewable in the dashboard, so a dead worker is visible instead of silent.

Cache: the restart signal is stored in the application cache, so the app's cache store must survive the restart (the file store does, inside one container).
